one_line_idea: Replacing distortion-to-reference with consistency-to-observation as the fidelity axis makes the perception tradeoff much milder, and consistency should be the reported fidelity metric for generative restoration.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Fidelity in SR is measured as distortion against one reference image, although for generative restorers the operationally meaningful constraint is agreement with the degraded observation under the forward model.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Perceptual quality conflicts strongly with single-reference distortion but only weakly with observation consistency, so reframing fidelity as data consistency reveals that high realism and high fidelity-to-evidence are jointly achievable.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across models, the correlation between perceptual quality and observation-consistency error will be much weaker than the correlation between perceptual quality and reference distortion, and some generative models will be near-perfectly consistent while scoring poorly on distortion.
why_important: It would legitimize generative restoration where it is evidence-consistent and expose it where it is not, replacing a misleading fidelity axis.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-consistency constraints are standard in inverse-problem solvers, but recasting the perception-distortion debate around measured consistency may be unexplored as an evaluation program.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For a set of restoration models with known or estimated forward operators, compute observation-consistency residuals and perceptual scores, and map the empirical tradeoff in the new axes.
main_risk: The forward operator is unknown for blind settings, making consistency measurement itself an estimation problem.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Distortion to the reference is treated as the definition of fidelity in restoration.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The reference is one posterior sample, not the evidence; penalizing distance to it punishes legitimate posterior diversity while missing genuine evidence violations.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-degrade outputs of several public models with the known synthetic forward operator and compare residual-to-observation against their reference distortion; discordance between the two fidelity notions is immediate evidence.

one_line_idea: Human-preferred restorations systematically degrade machine consumption (OCR, recognition), so perceptual quality and machine quality are diverging objectives needing separate outputs.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restored images are consumed both by humans and by downstream machine systems, while restoration models are tuned to human preference or its proxies.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Perceptually tuned restoration alters or destroys machine-relevant evidence (glyph shapes, fine boundaries, texture statistics) such that recognition systems perform worse on human-preferred restorations than on distortion-optimized ones of the same inputs.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across matched models, machine task accuracy on restored images will rank inversely with human preference on hallucination-prone content, with the gap concentrated in text and fine-structure regions.
why_important: Pipelines increasingly insert restoration before analysis; if perceptual tuning harms analysis, deployment guidance must change.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Task-driven restoration exists, but a systematic divergence study between human preference and machine accuracy across restoration operating points may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Restore a document-and-scene corpus with fidelity-oriented and perception-oriented models, run standard OCR and recognition systems, and correlate task accuracy with human preference scores.
main_risk: Divergence may vary strongly by task, complicating a clean general conclusion.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Better-looking restorations are assumed to be better inputs for downstream systems.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Human preference rewards plausible texture, but recognition depends on evidence preservation; texture synthesis and evidence preservation are different objectives that coincide only by accident.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run OCR on perceptually restored versus fidelity-restored low-quality text photos and compare character error rates; a consistent gap on a handful of images settles the direction quickly.

one_line_idea: Restoration models should output a hallucination map, and cross-seed variance of generative restorers already provides one that flags fabricated regions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Generative restoration outputs mix recovered evidence and prior-invented content with no indication of which is which.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-pixel dispersion across sampling seeds is a usable hallucination indicator: regions with high cross-seed variance are dominated by prior invention, and exposing this map materially changes user trust decisions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Cross-seed variance maps will overlap substantially with regions where outputs deviate from ground truth on synthetic tasks, and will flag most human-identified hallucinations on real tasks.
why_important: A standard hallucination-disclosure output would make generative restoration auditable, which matters for forensic, journalistic, and archival uses.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Sample diversity is studied as a quality, but standardizing seed-variance as a hallucination disclosure channel with validation against ground truth may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate multiple seeds per input on synthetic pairs, compute variance maps, and measure overlap with actual error maps; then validate on real images with human hallucination annotation.
main_risk: Consistently wrong regions (confident hallucination across seeds) evade the variance signal, so the map has a known blind spot.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Restoration outputs are presented as single images, with uncertainty communication considered out of scope.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Where evidence constrains the posterior, seeds agree; where the prior dominates, seeds disagree; this is exactly the recoverable-versus-invented distinction users need, available at zero training cost.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Sample a public diffusion restorer several times on one degraded face or text image, compute the pixel variance map, and check visually whether high-variance regions coincide with implausible or fabricated detail.

one_line_idea: Perceived restoration quality saturates under realistic viewing conditions, and beyond a resolvable-detail threshold the field is optimizing differences invisible to users.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration evaluation uses magnified crops and pixel-level metrics, while deployed images are viewed at finite display sizes, resolutions, and distances.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under representative viewing conditions, preference differences between recent top restoration models vanish for a large fraction of images, meaning reported improvements increasingly live below the visibility threshold.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Preference studies at realistic viewing scales will show no significant difference between models that differ clearly under magnified inspection, with the null result concentrating in mild-degradation images.
why_important: It calibrates how much of leaderboard progress delivers user-perceivable value and argues for viewing-condition-aware evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Psychophysics of display viewing is mature, but injecting viewing-condition realism into SR evaluation protocols may be rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Rerun pairwise comparisons of recent models under controlled realistic viewing (fixed display size and distance, no zoom) and measure how many previously significant gaps survive.
main_risk: Choosing representative viewing conditions is contestable, and results will vary across usage scenarios like print versus mobile.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Metric and crop-level improvements are assumed to translate into user-visible improvements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The human contrast sensitivity function imposes hard limits at typical angular resolutions; differences confined to frequencies beyond that limit cannot be seen regardless of their metric magnitude.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Display outputs of two recent models side by side at typical phone scale to a few viewers without zoom and count discrimination accuracy; chance-level discrimination on many images is quick evidence.

one_line_idea: Hallucination severity in generative SR scales with prior strength: the better the generative model, the more confidently it fabricates the wrong content.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Generative restoration combines observation evidence with a learned image prior, and stronger priors produce more plausible-looking detail.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] As the prior improves (more data, larger models), fabricated content becomes simultaneously more plausible and less faithful in evidence-poor regions, so semantic hallucination rate on ambiguous inputs increases with prior quality rather than decreasing.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across a scale ladder of generative restorers, human-verified semantic error rate on ambiguous inputs (unreadable text, small faces) will stay flat or rise with scale, while plausibility ratings of the same wrong content rise.
why_important: It contradicts the assumption that scaling fixes hallucination and implies restoration needs explicit evidence-tracking mechanisms, not just better priors.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Hallucination is widely acknowledged, but a controlled scaling study of hallucination severity in restoration may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or collect a capacity ladder of one restoration family, build an ambiguous-input evaluation set with known ground truth, and measure semantic error and plausibility versus scale.
main_risk: Semantic error annotation is labor-intensive and ambiguity levels must be carefully controlled for the trend to be interpretable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Better generative models are expected to hallucinate less because they know more about the world.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Where evidence is absent, the posterior is prior-dominated by definition; a stronger prior samples sharper, more convincing content, but the true content is unrecoverable, so conviction rises while accuracy cannot.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Restore identical barely-legible text crops with a weak and a strong public generative restorer and count legible-but-wrong outputs; more confident wrong text from the stronger model is the predicted signature.

one_line_idea: Face restoration homogenizes identity, drifting restored faces toward the training distribution's typical attributes, measurable as systematic embedding shift.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Face restoration models are trained on face datasets with specific demographic and photographic compositions, and severe degradation leaves identity underdetermined.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Restored faces exhibit a consistent drift in identity-embedding space toward dense regions of the training distribution, so restoration reduces inter-identity variance and biases perceived attributes toward the training majority.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Embedding distances between restored faces and their true identities will show a directional bias toward training-set attribute centroids, growing with degradation severity, and inter-identity embedding variance will shrink after restoration.
why_important: Identity distortion in face restoration has fairness, forensic, and personal-dignity implications, and the effect is invisible to standard quality metrics.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Identity preservation is measured as similarity to ground truth, but characterizing the direction of identity error as distribution-seeking drift may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Degrade faces of known identities at increasing severity, restore, compute identity embeddings, and test for directional drift toward training centroids and variance shrinkage.
main_risk: Face embedding models have their own biases, which must be controlled to avoid measuring the auditor instead of the restorer.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Identity errors in face restoration are assumed to be unbiased noise around the true identity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Under ambiguity, optimal samplers draw from the prior's dense regions; the prior is the training distribution, so errors must be systematically distribution-seeking rather than isotropic.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Restore heavily degraded faces of a few individuals with a public face restorer many times, average the embeddings, and check whether averaged restorations move consistently toward a common direction rather than scattering around the true identity.

one_line_idea: Late-stage sampling in diffusion-based SR is only weakly conditioned on the input, so the fine detail users see is mostly prior draw rather than evidence.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Diffusion restorers inject conditioning throughout the sampling trajectory, but the influence of conditioning on each stage of synthesis is not routinely measured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dependence of the output on the degraded input is concentrated in early, coarse-structure sampling stages, while late stages that synthesize fine texture are close to unconditional, meaning the visible detail is largely input-independent.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Swapping the conditioning image mid-trajectory will change coarse layout only when swapped early, and late-trajectory swaps will leave outputs nearly unchanged, demonstrating vanishing late-stage conditioning influence.
why_important: If fine detail is essentially unconditional, diffusion SR is texture synthesis with an evidence-shaped scaffold, which should change how it is evaluated and disclosed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Trajectory-stage analyses exist for generation, but quantifying stage-wise conditioning influence specifically for restoration fidelity may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Perform conditioning-swap and conditioning-ablation interventions at controlled trajectory points across many images, and measure output sensitivity as a function of intervention time.
main_risk: Results may vary across samplers and guidance mechanisms, requiring a broad matrix to generalize.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Conditioning is assumed to constrain synthesis uniformly through the trajectory.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Low-resolution evidence constrains low frequencies; once coarse structure is fixed, the remaining synthesis is dominated by the prior because the evidence has no high-frequency content to contribute.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On one public diffusion restorer, swap the conditioning image at a late sampling step and observe whether the output detail changes; near-identical outputs confirm weak late-stage conditioning within minutes.

one_line_idea: Sample diversity in stochastic restoration is misallocated: seeds vary irrelevant texture while collapsing on semantically ambiguous content where diversity actually matters.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Stochastic restorers advertise multiple plausible outputs as a feature representing posterior uncertainty.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-seed variation concentrates in perceptually irrelevant micro-texture while semantically ambiguous regions (which face, which character) collapse to a single mode, so the advertised diversity does not represent the true posterior where it counts.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Decomposing cross-seed variance into semantic and textural components will show textural variance dominating by a large factor, and constructed inputs with genuinely multimodal semantic posteriors will yield single-mode outputs across seeds.
why_important: Users interpreting sample spread as uncertainty will be misled precisely on high-stakes ambiguous content.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Diversity is reported as pixel spread; auditing whether diversity aligns with true posterior multimodality may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct degraded inputs consistent with several distinct semantic ground truths, sample restorers many times, and measure how often distinct semantic modes appear versus texture-only variation.
main_risk: Constructing verifiably multimodal inputs requires care; accidental evidence leakage would make mode collapse look correct.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Sample spread is presented and consumed as a proxy for posterior uncertainty.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mode-seeking training dynamics and guidance both suppress rare modes; texture has many near-equivalent optima while semantics has few distinct ones, so variance flows to texture by construction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Downsample an image containing a digit until ambiguous between two digits, sample a public restorer many times, and count whether both digits ever appear; persistent single-digit output demonstrates semantic collapse.

one_line_idea: Fixed default guidance scales in diffusion restoration are wrong for most images, and per-image guidance calibration from consistency residuals recovers substantial quality for free.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Diffusion restorers ship with a single guidance or conditioning-strength default that trades evidence adherence against prior-driven sharpness, applied uniformly across inputs.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The optimal guidance scale varies widely per image with degradation severity and content, and a cheap automatic calibrator that picks the scale by minimizing re-degradation residual plus a realism proxy beats any fixed scale on average.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Oracle per-image scale selection will beat the best fixed scale by a clear margin, and the automatic calibrator will capture most of that oracle gap.
why_important: It is an inference-time improvement requiring no retraining, applicable to all deployed diffusion restorers.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Guidance sensitivity is known, but closed-loop per-image guidance calibration for restoration via forward-model residuals may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep guidance per image on a benchmark to establish oracle gains, then implement residual-based automatic selection and measure the captured fraction of the oracle gap.
main_risk: The realism proxy in the selection objective could import metric-gaming biases into the calibrator.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A well-tuned global guidance default is assumed near-optimal across inputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Evidence strength varies by orders of magnitude across degradation severities; a single scale must over-trust the prior on mild inputs or under-trust it on severe ones.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For a handful of images at different severities, sweep the guidance scale of one public model and record the visually best setting per image; large per-image disagreement in best settings proves the fixed default is suboptimal.

one_line_idea: Cross-seed agreement in generative restoration is treated as certainty, but agreement can be confidently wrong, and the agreement-accuracy relationship has never been calibrated.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] When stochastic restorers produce consistent outputs across seeds, the consistency is naturally read as reliability, informally and in uncertainty heuristics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Conditional mode collapse makes seed agreement a miscalibrated certainty signal: a measurable fraction of high-agreement regions are systematically wrong, and the agreement-accuracy curve deviates far from the ideal.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On synthetic tasks with ground truth, binning pixels by cross-seed agreement will reveal substantial error mass in the highest-agreement bins, particularly in semantically ambiguous regions.
why_important: Seed-consensus is the most accessible uncertainty heuristic for generative restoration; if it is miscalibrated, downstream trust decisions built on it are unsafe.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Ensemble-agreement calibration is studied in classification; the analogous calibration audit for generative restoration consensus may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample restorers many times on synthetic degradations, compute per-region agreement, and plot agreement against ground-truth error to obtain a calibration curve.
main_risk: Results depend on the sampler's diversity settings, so audits must span sampling configurations to be conclusive.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Consistent outputs across seeds are assumed to indicate recovered rather than fabricated content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Guidance and mode-seeking dynamics collapse the sampled posterior to a narrow region that may exclude the truth entirely; agreement then measures collapse, not correctness.

one_line_idea: Generative restorers are unstable inverse maps: imperceptible input perturbations flip hallucinated semantic content, undermining forensic use.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Adversarial sensitivity is documented for classifiers, while restoration models are increasingly used to enhance evidentiary imagery.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Tiny, imperceptible perturbations of a degraded input can deterministically switch semantically meaningful restored content (different characters, different facial features), demonstrating that restored semantics are functions of noise-level input details no honest analyst would consider informative.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Gradient-based search will find perturbations far below visibility thresholds that change restored text or identity attributes in targeted directions, succeeding on most tested inputs.
why_important: If restored semantics can be steered by invisible input changes, restoration outputs must be inadmissible as evidence, and products need stability disclosures.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Adversarial attacks on SR exist for quality degradation; targeted semantic steering of hallucinated content in modern generative restorers may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define semantic targets (specific characters or attributes), run targeted perturbation search on degraded inputs against public restorers, and measure success rates and perturbation norms.
main_risk: Stochastic samplers complicate attack evaluation, requiring expectation-over-seeds attack objectives.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Restoration outputs are informally trusted as deterministic functions of visible input content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In evidence-poor regions the posterior is nearly flat, so infinitesimal input changes can move the sampled mode; instability is a structural property of prior-dominated inversion, not a bug.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Add tiny random perturbations (not even adversarial) to an ambiguous degraded text crop and re-restore; observing semantic flips across perturbations already demonstrates instability.

one_line_idea: Generative restorers can inject memorized training images into outputs on ambiguous inputs, and restoration needs a memorization-probe protocol like generation has.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Training-data memorization and regurgitation are documented in unconditional and text-conditional generative models, while restoration models trained on the same data families lack analogous audits.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When observation evidence is weak, restoration models sometimes complete inputs with near-copies of specific training images (faces, artworks, scenes), constituting a privacy and copyright hazard that current evaluation never surfaces.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Nearest-neighbor retrieval between restored outputs and the training corpus will uncover above-chance rates of high-similarity matches in evidence-poor regions, increasing with degradation severity and prior capacity.
why_important: Restoration is marketed as recovering the user's own content; injecting other people's memorized content is a qualitatively different and legally significant behavior.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Memorization audits exist for generation; a restoration-specific probe protocol conditioned on degradation severity may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Restore heavily degraded inputs with models whose training corpora are accessible, retrieve nearest training neighbors of outputs in feature space, and compare match rates against matched controls.
main_risk: Distinguishing memorized injection from generic prior knowledge requires careful similarity thresholds and controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Restoration models are assumed to synthesize generic detail rather than reproduce specific training instances.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Restoration training rewards exact reconstruction of training targets; under weak evidence the cheapest loss reduction is recalling training content, which is the definition of memorization pressure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Feed near-uninformative inputs (extreme downsampling) to a restorer trained on a known accessible corpus and retrieve nearest training neighbors of the outputs; conspicuous matches would appear in a small-scale probe.

judge_A_meta.master_note: memorization-privacy family: F-093 (generator memorization leaks training individuals) accepted for synthetic data; H-043 moves the hazard to restoration outputs. Also gen_n collision (N-081).

one_line_idea: The field needs a formal restoration-versus-reimagination boundary based on information recoverable from the observation, and most perceptual SR crosses it without disclosure.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration and generation are marketed as distinct, yet modern perceptual SR outputs contain large amounts of content not determined by the input observation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] An operational criterion comparing observation-derived information against prior-injected information per region can classify outputs into restoration and reimagination regimes, and applying it will show that popular perceptual SR operates mostly in the reimagination regime at high magnification factors.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Estimated prior-injected information share will exceed observation-derived share for most output content at large scale factors, with a sharp regime transition as magnification grows.
why_important: A disclosed, measurable boundary would let products and papers label outputs honestly and let regulation reference an operational standard.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The distinction is discussed philosophically, but an operational per-region information accounting for restoration may not have been formalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define estimators for observation-derived versus prior-injected information (via forward-model consistency and conditional entropy proxies), validate on synthetic cases with known ground truth, and apply to popular models across scale factors.
main_risk: Information estimates on images are approximation-heavy, and the boundary could be contested as estimator-dependent.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Perceptual SR is presented and consumed as restoration, with generation framing reserved for text-to-image tools.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At high magnification the observation contains a small fraction of the output's information content by simple counting arguments, so the output is necessarily mostly prior; the only question is making this measurable.
fastest_falsification_experiment: At increasing scale factors, measure how much output content survives when the conditioning is replaced by a different image with the same coarse structure; high survival indicates prior domination and locates the regime boundary cheaply.

one_line_idea: Text-to-image foundation priors import aesthetic bias into restoration: outputs drift toward beautified renditions rather than faithful ones.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration systems increasingly reuse text-to-image foundation models as priors, and those models are trained and tuned toward aesthetically pleasing outputs.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Foundation-prior restorers systematically shift outputs toward higher saturation, cleaner skin, tidier scenes, and removal of mundane imperfections relative to ground truth, a measurable aesthetic drift absent in task-trained restorers.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Paired comparisons on synthetic tasks will show foundation-prior restorers deviating from ground truth in consistent aesthetic directions (color statistics, skin smoothness, clutter reduction) significantly more than matched task-specific models.
why_important: Aesthetic drift is silent unfaithfulness: users receive prettier images that misrepresent reality, which matters for memories, documentation, and journalism.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Aesthetic tuning of generators is known, but quantifying its leakage into restoration fidelity as directional drift may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Restore synthetic degradations of unglamorous real scenes with foundation-prior and task-trained models, and measure directional deviations from ground truth along defined aesthetic axes.
main_risk: Defining aesthetic axes objectively is difficult, and some drift may come from degradation ambiguity rather than the prior.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Stronger foundation priors are assumed to make restoration strictly more accurate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The prior's mode is shaped by aesthetic preference tuning; under ambiguity the restorer samples near that mode, so beautification is the predictable direction of error, not random noise.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Restore a few deliberately mundane, imperfect photos (cluttered rooms, blemished skin) with a foundation-prior restorer and compare against ground truth for beautification; consistent prettifying on first examples confirms the drift direction.

one_line_idea: Vision-language-guided restoration converts caption errors into confident pixel hallucinations, a compounding error mode absent from caption-free restorers.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Some restoration pipelines condition on automatically generated captions or vision-language descriptions of the degraded input to inject semantic guidance.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When the captioner misreads degraded content, the restoration inherits and amplifies the error, rendering the wrong semantics with high visual confidence, so caption guidance is net-harmful on exactly the ambiguous inputs it was meant to help.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On inputs where the captioner errs, caption-guided restoration will produce more semantically wrong content than the same model without caption guidance, and total error will be dominated by caption-induced cases at high degradation severity.
why_important: Language-guided restoration is an appealing trend; identifying its compounding failure mode determines when it should be disabled.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Caption guidance is proposed for quality; an error-propagation analysis from captioner to pixels may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a caption-guided restorer with correct, automatically generated, and deliberately corrupted captions on synthetic degradations, and attribute semantic errors to caption versus image pathways.
main_risk: Guidance strength varies across implementations, so the effect size may be pipeline-specific.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Semantic guidance from language models is assumed to add robustness under severe degradation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The captioner sees the same degraded evidence the restorer does, so it adds no new information, only a hard semantic commitment made before pixel evidence is weighed.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Feed a caption-guided restorer a degraded image with a subtly wrong caption and observe whether the output follows the caption against the visual evidence; caption-following on a few examples demonstrates the pathway.

one_line_idea: Restoration quality saturates with model scale much earlier than generation quality because the task is observation-bounded, making restoration a poor showcase for foundation-scale compute.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Scaling model and data has produced dramatic gains in generative image modeling, and the restoration community increasingly adopts foundation-scale models expecting similar returns.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because restoration outputs are constrained by observation information, quality gains from scale saturate quickly once the prior suffices to fill the posterior, so scale ladders in restoration show early plateaus on fidelity metrics even as generation metrics keep improving.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A matched scale ladder will show fidelity-relevant restoration metrics plateauing at moderate scale, while unconditional generation quality of the same backbones continues improving, dissociating the two trends.
why_important: It informs resource allocation: if restoration saturates early, deployment should favor small distilled models and effort should go to degradation modeling instead of scale.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scaling laws exist for generation and recognition; a careful restoration-specific scaling study separating fidelity from realism may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a capacity ladder of one restoration architecture on fixed data, measure fidelity and realism metrics separately versus scale, and locate plateaus per metric family and degradation severity.
main_risk: Realism metrics may keep improving with scale, tempting misreading of the plateau claim, which specifically concerns evidence-bounded fidelity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Foundation-scale priors are assumed to keep improving restoration the way they improve generation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Once the prior can represent all images consistent with the observation, extra capacity refines preferences among indistinguishable options; fidelity cannot improve because the evidence bottleneck, not the prior, binds.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare small, medium, and large checkpoints of one public restoration family on mild degradations; near-identical fidelity outcomes at visibly different compute already indicate early saturation.

one_line_idea: Universal all-in-one restoration models suffer negative transfer on hard cases, losing to per-task specialists at matched capacity despite average-metric parity.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Foundation-style restoration models advertise a single network handling denoising, deblurring, SR, and inpainting, reporting strong averaged benchmark results.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Multi-task restoration training induces negative transfer concentrated in the hardest quantiles of each task, so all-in-one models match specialists on averages while losing clearly on per-task tail performance, which averages hide.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Quantile-stratified evaluation will show all-in-one models underperforming matched-capacity specialists in the worst-decile inputs of each task, even where mean metrics tie.
why_important: Tail performance drives user-perceived reliability; if generalists lose the tail, the all-in-one trend trades invisible-but-real quality for convenience.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multi-task interference is studied broadly, but tail-focused audits of universal restoration models may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train specialists and an all-in-one model at matched capacity and data per task, then compare full quantile curves rather than means on each task.
main_risk: Capacity matching between one generalist and several specialists is definitionally ambiguous and needs multiple fairness conventions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Unified restoration models are assumed to benefit from cross-task synergy with negligible interference.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Restoration tasks demand conflicting inverse operators on similar local patterns (sharpen edges versus suppress noise), and conflicts bind hardest where inputs are most ambiguous, which is exactly the tail.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one public all-in-one model against one public specialist on the specialist's task, sorting results by difficulty; inspect the hardest examples for a systematic generalist deficit.

one_line_idea: Self-supervised foundation features are worse perceptual-loss backbones than older supervised features because SSL objectives explicitly learn invariances that a fidelity metric must not have.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Perceptual losses compare images in a feature space, and the field is replacing classification-pretrained backbones with self-supervised foundation backbones on the assumption that better features make better losses.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Augmentation-invariance training makes SSL features blind to exactly the shifts, recolorings, and local deformations that restoration losses must penalize, so SSL-feature losses train models with more geometric and color drift than classification-feature losses.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Restorers trained with SSL-feature losses will exhibit measurably more spatial drift and color deviation from ground truth than those trained with supervised-feature losses, at matched perceptual sharpness.
why_important: Loss backbone choice is quietly consequential; adopting foundation features by prestige rather than by loss-suitability could degrade fidelity across the field.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Perceptual-loss backbone comparisons exist, but an invariance-theoretic account predicting which backbones fail as fidelity losses may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure feature sensitivity of candidate backbones to controlled shifts, color changes, and deformations; train matched restorers with each as loss backbone; correlate backbone invariance with output drift.
main_risk: Feature-layer choice within each backbone may matter more than the pretraining objective, requiring layer-controlled comparisons.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Stronger representation learners are assumed to provide strictly better perceptual losses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A loss should penalize any deviation from the target; invariance is anti-correlated with that requirement by design, and SSL training maximizes invariance to the nuisance family.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute feature distances of an SSL backbone and a supervised backbone under small translations and color shifts of the same image; near-zero SSL distances under changes a fidelity loss must catch demonstrate the unsuitability directly.

judge_A_meta.anomaly_note: SSL invariances make foundation features WORSE perceptual-loss backbones than older supervised features — inverts the newer-features-are-better default

one_line_idea: A systematic failure atlas of foundation-model restoration would show failures concentrating where the prior is strongest and the evidence weakest, inverting the intuition that strong priors help most on hard content.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Foundation-model restorers are evaluated by aggregate metrics, while their failures (wrong text, altered faces, bent straight lines, broken repeated patterns) are reported anecdotally.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Failure density is predictable from a two-factor map of prior confidence and evidence strength: high-prior low-evidence regions (faces, text, familiar objects under severe degradation) fail at the highest rates, while low-prior regions degrade gracefully.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A content-stratified audit will show semantic error rates ordered by prior-strength-over-evidence ratio, with structured content under severe degradation failing far more often than unfamiliar textures under the same degradation.
why_important: A validated failure map enables risk-aware deployment (route or abstain on high-risk regions) and gives the field a shared taxonomy for progress tracking.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Failure examples circulate widely, but a quantitative two-factor failure atlas for restoration may not have been constructed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define content strata with proxy measures of prior strength and evidence strength, run foundation restorers across a severity sweep, and fit failure rate against the two factors.
main_risk: Prior-strength proxies are debatable, and the atlas may not transfer across model families.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Strong priors are assumed to help most exactly where evidence is weakest.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Where evidence is weak the prior fills in aggressively; strong priors fill in confidently and specifically, so the cost of being wrong is highest where the prior is most opinionated.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare restoration failure rates on severely degraded faces versus equally degraded random textures for one public model; a large face-versus-texture semantic error gap sketches the atlas in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: In-context restoration examples act as style anchors rather than degradation evidence: shuffled or mismatched example pairs work nearly as well as correct ones.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] In-context restoration systems accept example degraded-clean pairs at inference, claimed to specify the degradation to invert.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models mostly ignore the degradation relationship inside example pairs and use them as output-style references, so deliberately mismatched examples (wrong degradation, unrelated content) reduce performance far less than the in-context framing predicts.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Replacing correct example pairs with degradation-mismatched pairs will cause only a small performance drop, while removing style information from the examples will cause a comparable or larger drop.
why_important: If examples are style anchors, in-context restoration's claimed few-shot degradation adaptation is illusory, and interface design should change accordingly.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] In-context ability is asserted via benchmark gains; causal ablations of what the examples contribute may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Factorially vary example correctness (right degradation, wrong degradation, right style, wrong style) and measure performance attribution across factors.
main_risk: Different in-context architectures may use examples differently, limiting generality of any single audit.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Example pairs are assumed to convey the degradation operator that the model then inverts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Inferring an operator from one pair and applying its inverse is a hard compositional skill, while copying output statistics is an easy shortcut; models trained by gradient descent take the shortcut when it pays equally on the training distribution.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Give one public in-context restorer a query image with example pairs from a different degradation type and compare against correct examples; a negligible gap on a handful of images exposes the shortcut.

one_line_idea: Repeated passes through neural processing (restoration, editing, recompression) create a compounding neural degradation family that classic degradation models cannot express, and future restorers must model it explicitly.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Images increasingly traverse multiple neural systems (enhancement on device, platform recompression, editing tools) before any restoration attempt, while degradation pipelines model only classic physical and codec operators.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Iterated neural processing produces distinctive compounding artifacts (statistics drift, over-regularized texture, semantic residue from earlier edits) that classic pipelines never synthesize, and restorers trained with simulated neural-processing chains will beat classic-pipeline models on such content.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On corpora of multiply-processed images, chain-trained models will outperform classic-pipeline models by a clear margin, while the two will remain comparable on single-degradation content.
why_important: The share of multiply-neural-processed imagery is growing without bound; a degradation model of neural processing itself may become the core of practical restoration.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Recompression chains are studied in forensics, but treating iterated neural enhancement as a synthesizable degradation family for restoration training may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build processing chains from public enhancement and compression models, generate chain-degraded training data, train matched models, and evaluate on genuinely multiply-processed real images.
main_risk: The space of neural processing chains is vast and version-dependent, so simulated chains may not cover deployed ones.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Blur, noise, resampling, and codec artifacts are assumed to remain a sufficient degradation basis.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Neural processors introduce structured, learned biases that are content-adaptive; no combination of independent stochastic classic stages reproduces the statistics of a learned operator's output manifold.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Pass images through a few rounds of public enhance-then-compress cycles, run a classic-pipeline restorer, and compare with its behavior on classic degradations of matched severity; distinctive failure on chain-processed inputs is quick to observe.

one_line_idea: Standard SR ground truths are themselves degraded, imposing a hidden quality ceiling and penalizing models that exceed ground-truth quality.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] High-resolution reference images in common SR datasets were captured with real cameras and pipelines, so they contain their own noise, compression, sharpening halos, and optical softness.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable fraction of reference images in standard benchmarks contains visible degradations, and models producing cleaner-than-reference outputs are systematically penalized by full-reference metrics, distorting method rankings near the quality ceiling.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A ground-truth quality audit will find a nontrivial share of degraded references, and re-evaluating on a verified-clean subset will change method rankings among top models.
why_important: As models approach reference quality, reference flaws dominate measurement; the field may already be ranking models by how well they reproduce reference defects.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual dataset complaints exist, but a systematic reference-quality audit with re-ranking analysis across benchmarks may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Have annotators and no-reference metrics grade reference quality across standard benchmarks, construct a clean subset, and compare model rankings between full sets and clean subsets.
main_risk: Clean-subset selection could itself bias content distribution, confounding the re-ranking.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark references are treated as clean gold standards by construction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every reference was produced by some acquisition pipeline with its own degradation; the notion of a degradation-free photograph is physically incoherent, only degrees of cleanliness exist.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Zoom into references of one popular benchmark and count images with visible compression blocks, noise, or sharpening halos; finding several within the first dozens demonstrates the ceiling issue.

judge_A_meta.master_note: reference-quality family: C-025 (annotation error exceeds model gaps), B-091 (label-entropy floors); H-055's regression-substrate ceiling (degraded GT penalizes cleaner-than-reference outputs) is the delta.

one_line_idea: Luma-only PSNR evaluation lets SR models neglect chroma, and hidden color artifacts are widespread but unmeasured.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A long-standing convention evaluates SR on the luminance channel only, on the rationale that human vision is luminance-dominated.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models tuned under luma-only evaluation systematically underperform on chroma reconstruction (color bleeding, desaturation of fine structure, hue shifts at edges), and full-color evaluation would reorder methods and expose a neglected error family.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Chroma-specific error metrics will show model differences larger than luma differences among top methods, and human raters will spot color artifacts in a nontrivial fraction of outputs judged clean by luma metrics.
why_important: Color fidelity matters for products and archival use; a convention that hides an entire error dimension distorts both research and deployment choices.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The luma convention is occasionally questioned, but a systematic chroma-error audit of the modern method panel may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate a panel of published models with chroma-aware metrics and targeted human inspection of color artifacts, comparing rankings against luma-only results.
main_risk: Chroma metrics are less standardized, inviting disputes about metric choice rather than about the finding.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Luma-only evaluation is assumed to capture everything perceptually significant in SR quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optimization goes where measurement is; decades of luma-only measurement predict systematic chroma neglect as a straightforward incentive consequence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute per-channel error maps for a few public models and inspect edges of colorful objects for bleeding and hue shifts invisible in the luma channel; examples typically surface quickly if the effect is real.

one_line_idea: No-reference quality metrics actively reward hallucination in generative SR because modern fabrication artifacts lie outside their training distortion domains.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real-world SR without references is evaluated with no-reference quality models trained on legacy distortion types like blur, noise, and compression.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Since fabricated detail is sharp and natural-looking locally, no-reference metrics score hallucinated outputs above faithful ones, so optimizing or ranking by these metrics selects for confident fabrication.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On synthetic tasks with ground truth, no-reference scores will correlate positively with hallucination measures among generative restorers, and metric-ranked leaderboards will invert human fidelity-aware rankings.
why_important: No-reference metrics gatekeep the real-world SR literature; if they reward the central failure mode, the subfield's measured progress is partly the growth of that failure.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Metric limitations are acknowledged generally, but demonstrating a systematic pro-hallucination bias of no-reference metrics may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct output sets with controlled hallucination levels at fixed low-level quality, score them with popular no-reference metrics, and measure the score-versus-hallucination relationship.
main_risk: Controlling hallucination level independently of low-level quality is experimentally delicate.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] No-reference metrics are treated as imperfect but directionally sound quality proxies.
why_it_might_be_wrong: These metrics were trained to detect legacy distortions; fabrication removes such distortions while adding semantic falsehood the metrics have no channel to sense, so the score can only improve.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Score a faithful-but-soft restoration and a sharp-but-fabricated restoration of the same input with popular no-reference metrics; consistent preference for fabrication across a few examples exposes the bias.

one_line_idea: Crop-based human studies over-sample regions where hallucination looks good, and whole-image task-driven protocols would flip some perceptual-SR conclusions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Human evaluations in SR papers typically show small crops selected to exhibit visible differences, often texture-rich regions, under forced-choice preference.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Crop selection biases studies toward stochastic-texture regions where fabricated detail wins, while whole-image viewing and task-driven judgments (would you trust or share this photo) weight semantic fidelity higher and would reverse some published preferences.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The same model pairs will show significantly different preference outcomes between curated-crop protocols and whole-image or task-framed protocols, with reversals concentrated on hallucination-prone content.
why_important: Human studies are the court of final appeal in perceptual SR; protocol-induced verdicts steer the field's objectives.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Protocol effects are studied in quality assessment broadly, but crop-selection bias in SR studies may be unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Rerun comparisons for several model pairs under crop-based, whole-image, and task-framed protocols with matched raters, and measure verdict stability across protocols.
main_risk: Task framing introduces its own variability and requires careful instruction design.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Preference on informative crops is assumed to generalize to whole-image judgments.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Crops remove context that reveals inconsistency and stakes; a fabricated texture patch is pleasing in isolation but suspicious inside a full scene where it mismatches neighboring evidence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For a few images, collect preferences on the paper-style best crop and on the full image from the same raters; disagreement between the two verdicts on the sample is quick evidence.

one_line_idea: Real degradation severity is bimodal (mostly mild plus a hard tail) while benchmarks concentrate on mid-range severity, so deployment-weighted evaluation would change model choices.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark degradation parameters are chosen to be challenging and discriminative, without reference to measured deployment severity distributions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The severity distribution of real user photos is strongly bimodal, and model rankings under deployment-weighted severity sampling differ from mid-severity benchmark rankings, favoring models with good mild-case identity behavior and robust hard-tail behavior over mid-range specialists.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Estimating a deployment severity distribution and reweighting evaluation accordingly will reorder a model panel relative to standard benchmarks, with mild-input artifact behavior becoming a deciding factor.
why_important: Products serve the deployment distribution, not the benchmark distribution; misweighted evaluation systematically selects wrong models for real use.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Severity realism is discussed for individual datasets, but deployment-weighted evaluation as a general protocol for restoration may be unformalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate severity distributions from large real photo corpora with no-reference degradation estimators, build a weighted evaluation protocol, and compare panel rankings against standard benchmarks.
main_risk: Severity estimation error and corpus selection bias could distort the deployment distribution estimate.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Mid-to-high severity benchmarks are assumed to be conservative proxies covering practical needs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A benchmark that never measures the mild regime cannot detect over-restoration harms there, and the mild regime is where most real images live, so the blind spot covers the majority of deployment volume.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run a no-reference severity estimator over a personal photo library and plot the histogram; observing the mild-heavy bimodal shape immediately questions mid-severity benchmark weighting.

one_line_idea: Expected-distortion evaluation of stochastic restorers penalizes legitimate posterior diversity, and set-based or distributional fidelity metrics are required to compare generative restoration fairly.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Stochastic restorers output samples from a conditional distribution, yet benchmarks score a single sample against a single reference with alignment-sensitive metrics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Single-sample-versus-single-reference scoring systematically misranks stochastic methods (penalizing honest diversity, rewarding mode-averaged blur or collapse), and set-level protocols (best-of-k, coverage-precision over samples, distributional distance to a reference set) change conclusions about which generative restorer is better.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Rankings of stochastic restorers under set-based protocols will disagree materially with single-sample rankings, with the disagreement growing with output diversity.
why_important: The field is comparing distribution-valued outputs with point-valued tools; wrong tools mean wrong winners and wrong research directions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Best-of-k reporting appears occasionally, but a principled evaluation framework for distributional restoration outputs may be unestablished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several stochastic restorers under single-sample, best-of-k, and distributional protocols on synthetic tasks, and quantify ranking disagreement across protocols.
main_risk: Set-based protocols have their own gameability (diversity inflation for best-of-k), requiring guardrails in protocol design.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Single-sample scoring is assumed adequate because users see one output.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For multimodal posteriors, the best single deterministic answer differs from any honest sample; scoring samples as if they were deterministic predictions structurally punishes correctness about uncertainty.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare two public stochastic restorers under single-sample and best-of-five scoring on one synthetic set; a rank flip between protocols demonstrates the issue with minimal compute.

one_line_idea: Training restoration losses in gamma-encoded sRGB misweights shadow and highlight errors, and linear-light loss computation changes model behavior visibly in low light.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration losses are almost universally computed on gamma-encoded pixel values, although physical light mixing and sensor noise operate in linear space.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Gamma-space losses over-weight shadow errors and under-weight highlight errors relative to physical error, biasing models toward shadow smoothing and highlight neglect, and computing losses in approximately linearized space yields visibly different, tonally better-balanced restorations.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Matched models trained with gamma-space and linear-space losses will differ systematically in shadow detail retention and highlight artifact rates, with human preference favoring the linear-trained model on low-light content.
why_important: This is a zero-cost training change touching every restoration model; if the encoding choice matters, the default has been silently shaping all results.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Linear-versus-gamma processing is standard knowledge in graphics, but a controlled study of loss-space encoding effects on learned restoration may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with losses computed in sRGB, approximately linearized, and perceptually uniform spaces, and compare tonal-region-stratified errors and human preferences.
main_risk: Without true linear ground truth (raw data), linearization is approximate and could blunt the effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Loss-space encoding is treated as an irrelevant implementation detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The gamma curve reallocates numeric error weight across tones by design; a loss inherits that reallocation whether or not it matches perceptual or physical importance, so the choice cannot be neutral.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one small model with a linearized loss and inspect low-light outputs against the sRGB-trained baseline; tonal behavior differences on a handful of night photos indicate the effect size.

one_line_idea: The field optimizes 4x magnification while deployment overwhelmingly needs mild continuous scales, and mild-scale performance is not predicted by 4x benchmark scores.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] SR research standardized on integer scale factors, with 4x as the flagship setting, while practical zoom, display fitting, and print needs concentrate on modest continuous factors.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model quality at mild continuous scales correlates weakly with 4x benchmark scores because mild-scale quality is dominated by resampling finesse and identity preservation rather than by texture synthesis, so the community's flagship metric does not measure the practically dominant regime.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A panel ranked at 4x will show substantially different ordering at mild continuous scales, with some 4x leaders producing visible artifacts at small factors where subtle resampling wins.
why_important: If the flagship setting mismatches deployment, research incentives are pulling models away from what users actually need.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Arbitrary-scale SR is an active topic, but an explicit audit showing rank divergence between flagship and deployment-typical scales may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a broad model panel across a dense grid of scale factors, compute cross-scale rank correlations, and identify the scale regimes where rankings decouple.
main_risk: Ground-truth construction at continuous scales requires careful resampling protocols to avoid biasing toward particular methods.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Performance at 4x is assumed to upper-bound and predict performance at easier smaller scales.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Small factors demand near-identity behavior where over-synthesis is a liability; a model optimized to invent texture at 4x has been trained toward the opposite disposition.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run a few 4x-flagship models at a mild continuous scale on clean images and inspect for over-sharpening and texture invention; artifacts at mild scales from 4x leaders make the decoupling concrete.

one_line_idea: High-resolution training targets contain sensor noise that models learn to reproduce, so part of learned texture synthesis is actually noise imitation, and denoised-target training changes the perceptual character of outputs.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] SR training pairs use captured photographs as targets, and captured photographs contain noise and grain, especially in texture-rich regions where SR models are said to synthesize detail.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable component of what perceptual SR models render as fine texture is learned reproduction of target noise statistics, and training against carefully denoised targets yields models whose outputs look different in texture character while scoring similarly on structure.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Matched models trained on original versus denoised targets will differ in output micro-texture statistics, with the original-target model's texture matching the noise spectrum of the training targets.
why_important: It reframes some claimed detail synthesis as noise imitation and gives practitioners a controllable knob (target cleaning) over output character.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Target quality is occasionally mentioned, but attributing synthesized texture to target noise spectra with controlled experiments may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build training sets with original and strongly denoised targets, train matched models, and compare output texture spectra against the respective target noise spectra.
main_risk: Aggressive denoising removes genuine fine detail from targets, confounding noise removal with detail removal.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Target images are treated as noise-free representations of desired output.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The loss cannot distinguish target noise from target detail; matching the target distribution necessarily includes matching its noise, so noise imitation is a predictable training outcome.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare the high-frequency spectrum of one perceptual model's outputs in flat regions against the noise spectrum of its known training targets; spectral alignment in flat regions suggests noise imitation directly.

one_line_idea: Real degradations vary strongly across the frame, and globally-conditioned restoration produces spatially inconsistent quality that per-region degradation conditioning fixes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Optical blur grows toward frame corners, defocus varies with depth, and vignetting changes local noise visibility, yet most blind restorers estimate at most one global degradation state per image.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On real photos, spatial degradation variance is large enough that global conditioning leaves corner regions under-restored and center regions over-restored (or vice versa), and spatially-varying degradation estimation with per-region conditioning yields consistent quality across the frame.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Quality maps of globally-conditioned restorations on real photos will show systematic center-versus-corner gradients, which shrink substantially under spatially-varying conditioning at matched capacity.
why_important: Frame-consistent quality is a product requirement (users crop corners too), and the fix is an estimation-design change rather than more capacity.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Spatially variant degradation is modeled in deblurring niches, but quantifying the global-conditioning penalty for general real-world restoration may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure spatial degradation variance on a real corpus, train matched models with global and spatial conditioning, and compare spatial quality-uniformity statistics.
main_risk: Spatial degradation estimation is noisy at fine granularity, and estimation errors could introduce new inconsistencies.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-image global degradation states are assumed adequate because within-image variation is treated as minor.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Lens physics guarantees field-position dependence and scene depth guarantees defocus variation; a single global state is wrong for essentially every real photograph, the only question is by how much.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Estimate blur locally in center and corner patches across a handful of real photos; consistently larger corner blur quantifies the variance a global state ignores.

one_line_idea: Restoration models exploit the correlation between content and degradation in real data as a shortcut, and they misrestore counterfactual images where the correlation is broken.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] In real corpora, degradation correlates with content: night scenes are noisy, telephoto shots are soft, indoor images are high-ISO, and training data inherits these correlations.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models learn content-conditioned degradation expectations (denoise night scenes hard, sharpen distant subjects) and apply them even when actual degradation contradicts the content prior, producing systematic errors on counterfactual inputs like clean night photos or noisy daylight photos.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On constructed counterfactual pairs (same content, atypical degradation), models will apply the content-typical correction rather than the evidence-indicated one, with error patterns tracking the training correlation structure.
why_important: Shortcut degradation inference undermines trust: the model's treatment depends on what the scene looks like rather than on measurable degradation evidence.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Shortcut learning is documented for recognition; content-degradation shortcuts in restoration may be unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build counterfactual test sets crossing content type with degradation type against the natural correlation, and measure whether restoration strength follows evidence or content.
main_risk: Constructing convincing counterfactuals (truly clean night photos) requires careful capture work.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Blind models are assumed to infer degradation from degradation evidence, with content serving only as restoration context.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Content is an easier, more predictive feature for the training distribution than subtle degradation cues; gradient descent prefers the easy predictive path, which is the definition of shortcut formation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Feed a blind restorer a tripod-captured clean night scene and a noise-injected daylight scene; over-denoising the clean night shot and under-denoising the noisy day shot reveals the shortcut in two images.

one_line_idea: Tiled inference silently degrades large-image restoration through seam artifacts and context truncation, and patch-benchmark scores hide a whole-image quality gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Deployed restoration runs on large images via overlapping tiles for memory reasons, while benchmarks evaluate on small crops that fit in a single forward pass.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Tiling introduces measurable quality loss (blending softness at seams, inconsistent hallucination across tiles, loss of global context for degradation estimation) that patch benchmarks never register, so deployed quality is systematically below benchmarked quality in a size-dependent way.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing whole-pass and tiled inference of the same model on large images will show consistent quality loss for tiling, growing as tile size shrinks and degradation estimation becomes more local.
why_important: Benchmark-to-product quality gaps erode trust; quantifying the tiling tax would push architecture research toward memory-efficient global-context inference.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Tiling artifacts are practitioner folklore; a systematic measurement of the tiling tax across models and tile sizes may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select models capable of whole-pass inference on large images, compare whole-pass against tiled outputs across tile-size grids, and characterize seam and consistency errors.
main_risk: Whole-pass inference at large sizes may itself behave off-distribution if models were trained on crops, entangling two effects.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Overlapping-tile blending is assumed to make tiled inference equivalent to whole-image inference.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Blind restoration needs global evidence (noise level, blur extent) that a small tile cannot supply, and stochastic synthesis makes neighboring tiles disagree; blending averages disagreements into visible softness rather than removing them.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Restore one large image whole and tiled with a public model and difference the results; structured disagreement along tile boundaries visualizes the tax immediately.

one_line_idea: Training against a single ground-truth realization teaches models false confidence at high magnification, and the one-target assumption is the root of both blur (regression) and overconfident fabrication (generation).
problem: [KNOWN FACT] SR training treats the particular high-resolution capture as the unique correct answer, although at high magnification many distinct images are equally consistent with the input.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The single-target convention is the common cause of the field's two signature pathologies: pixel losses average over the unacknowledged posterior (blur), and adversarial or diffusion losses pick one mode and present it as the answer (overconfident fabrication); training objectives that explicitly acknowledge target multiplicity (multi-target supervision where obtainable, posterior-aware losses) reduce both pathologies simultaneously.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On synthetic tasks where multiple valid targets can be constructed per input, multi-target-trained models will show less blur than regression baselines and less confident fabrication than single-target generative baselines.
why_important: It locates a shared root cause beneath problems usually treated separately, suggesting one fix rather than two patches.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Posterior framing is standard theory, but constructing genuinely multi-target supervision for SR and testing the two-pathology prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate synthetic inputs each consistent with several constructed ground truths, train models under single-target and multi-target objectives, and measure blur and fabrication pathologies separately.
main_risk: Constructing valid multi-target supervision at scale is expensive and may only be feasible for synthetic content families.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The single ground truth per input is treated as definitional for supervised restoration.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The forward operator is many-to-one; pretending it is one-to-one forces every training signal to misrepresent the inverse problem, and the misrepresentation must surface as some pathology.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On a toy family (rendered patterns downsampled with heavy information loss), train with one versus several valid targets per input and compare output behavior; the contrast typically appears at small scale quickly.

judge_A_meta.anomaly_note: the single-ground-truth training convention is the common root cause of both regression blur and generative overconfident fabrication

one_line_idea: Eight-bit quantization of training pairs imposes an ignored information floor, causing banding-related failure modes and capping low-contrast detail recovery that higher-bit-depth training would unlock.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard SR training and evaluation use 8-bit images for both input and target, while sensors capture 10 to 14 bits and displays increasingly render more than 8 bits.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Quantization noise and banding in 8-bit training data teach models to reproduce or amplify banding in smooth gradients and to ignore sub-quantization-level structure, and training on higher-bit-depth pairs measurably improves smooth-gradient rendering and low-contrast texture recovery.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Matched models trained at 8-bit and higher bit depth will differ visibly on smooth gradients (sky, skin) with the high-bit model showing less banding and better low-contrast texture, even when evaluated at 8-bit output.
why_important: Bit depth is a silent pipeline default touching all training data; if it caps quality on smooth regions, a cheap data-pipeline change improves every model.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Bit depth is standard in HDR research, but its role as a quality ceiling for ordinary SR training may be unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build raw-derived training pairs at multiple bit depths, train matched models, and evaluate banding metrics and low-contrast detail recovery per tonal region.
main_risk: Gains may be invisible under 8-bit evaluation pipelines, requiring end-to-end higher-bit evaluation to detect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Eight bits are assumed perceptually sufficient, making bit depth a non-factor for restoration research.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Restoration amplifies subtle gradients where 8-bit steps are near visibility; a model cannot learn to render gradients smoother than its targets ever were.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inspect smooth-gradient regions of current model outputs for banding inherited from quantized targets; finding characteristic step patterns in skies across models suggests the ceiling is active.
