one_line_idea: Attribute-binding failures are decided in a narrow early timestep window through cross-attention competition, so timestep-targeted attention intervention fixes most binding errors while leaving the rest of generation untouched.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Text-to-image models routinely swap or merge attributes between objects ('red cube, blue sphere' comes out wrong), and existing fixes apply global attention manipulation across all steps.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Binding is resolved when object regions first individuate (early, high-noise steps); attribute tokens compete for regions only in that window, so interventions confined to it capture the full fixable fraction of binding failures at minimal collateral cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Attention intervention restricted to the first quarter of steps will recover at least 80% of the binding-accuracy improvement of full-schedule intervention while reducing off-target image change by 50%+; kill if late-window intervention performs within 10% of early-window (no temporal specificity).
why_important: Localizing when binding happens converts a bag of attention tricks into a mechanism statement about compositional generation, and cheapens every binding fix.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Attention-based binding fixes exist by recall; a temporal-specificity dissociation with pre-registered windows appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a benchmark of two-object attribute prompts, apply the same attention intervention in early, middle, late, and full windows, scoring binding accuracy with detectors/VQA and off-target change with masked perceptual metrics.
main_risk: Binding may be re-negotiated at middle steps for some prompt structures, splitting the window and complicating the clean story.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Binding failure is treated as a static representational deficiency of the text encoder or attention design, not a temporally localized decision.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If binding errors originate in the text embedding itself, no attention-timing intervention will show temporal specificity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Window ablations over ~2k prompts: under a day on one GPU with public models.

one_line_idea: Object-count control fails because count is not linearly represented anywhere in the conditioning pathway beyond small numbers: probing text and image streams will find count decodable up to about four and absent beyond, matching the generation failure boundary.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Text-to-image models are unreliable at generating requested object counts beyond a handful, and the failure is usually attributed vaguely to 'poor compositionality'.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The failure is representational: the conditioning pathway encodes numerosity like a subitizing system (distinct up to ~4, log-compressed beyond), so generation cannot execute counts its representation does not distinguish; probe decodability and generation accuracy will share the same breakpoint.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Linear probes for requested count on text-encoder and cross-attention representations will show accuracy falling below 60% beyond count 4-5 exactly where generation count-accuracy collapses, with the two breakpoints within 1 unit; kill if representations remain decodable (85%+) at counts where generation fails.
why_important: Locating the bottleneck (representation versus execution) decides whether count control needs better text encoders or better sampling-time grounding, two entirely different research programs.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Counting failures are benchmarked; the representational-breakpoint alignment test appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build count-controlled prompts, probe count decodability at multiple pipeline stages, measure generation count accuracy with detectors, and compare breakpoint locations.
main_risk: Detector counting errors at high counts could blur the generation breakpoint; validate detectors on rendered ground-truth scenes first.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Counting failure is attributed to insufficient compositional training data rather than a specific representational format limit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Count may be decodable but not causally used by the denoiser, in which case probes pass while generation fails and the bottleneck is execution.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Probing plus ~3k generations with automated counting: a few hours on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Prompt token influence follows a lawful positional decay: later tokens in long prompts lose per-token causal effect on the image at a measurable rate, and re-normalizing attention by position recovers late-token content without retraining.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Users observe that content mentioned late in long prompts often fails to appear, but token-position effects on generation have no quantitative characterization or principled fix.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Softmax attention over many tokens dilutes per-token mass with prompt length and position (compounded by causal text-encoder biases), producing a measurable positional influence decay that a position-corrected attention rescaling can flatten.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Causal token-deletion tests will show late-quartile tokens having at least 40% less image effect than early-quartile tokens in 60+ token prompts, and positional rescaling will recover late-token content realization by 25%+ relative without harming early content by more than 5%; kill if positional decay is under 15% (no meaningful effect).
why_important: Prompt-position inequity silently shapes what users can express, and a training-free flattening fix would immediately improve long-prompt reliability.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Long-prompt neglect is folklore; a causal positional-influence curve plus a rescaling correction appears unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct long prompts with position-permuted content units, measure realization of each unit via detectors/VQA across positions, fit the decay curve, then evaluate attention-rescaling corrections.
main_risk: Content units differ in realizability; permutation designs must balance unit difficulty across positions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Prompt neglect is attributed to model capacity or prompt quality, not to a systematic positional mechanism.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The text encoder may already equalize positions via bidirectional attention, putting the neglect elsewhere (e.g., content competition, not position).
fastest_falsification_experiment: Permutation battery over ~1k prompts: a few hours on one GPU.

one_line_idea: The same concept prompted in different languages generates measurably different visual distributions, and the differences are systematic (cultural-visual priors of the training pairs), quantifying language as a hidden conditioning variable in multilingual models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multilingual text-to-image usage assumes translation-equivalent prompts produce equivalent imagery, but caption corpora pair each language with culturally distinct image distributions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The conditioning pathway binds each language's tokens to that language's co-occurring visual statistics, so translation-equivalent prompts yield distribution-level differences (objects, settings, aesthetics) far exceeding sampling noise, predictable from corpus provenance.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Classifier two-sample tests between generation sets from translation-equivalent prompts will exceed 60% accuracy (50% null) for at least half of tested concept-language pairs, with shift directions consistent with corpus provenance in blind human ratings; kill if distributions are indistinguishable (under 53%) for most pairs.
why_important: Language-conditioned distribution shift affects fairness, localization products, and any evaluation using translated prompts, and it measures how conditioning entangles semantics with data provenance.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Anecdotes about language-dependent style exist; a systematic two-sample quantification across concepts and languages appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate matched sets for concept prompts across 4+ languages, run two-sample tests and attribute-level comparisons, and validate shift interpretability with small human ratings.
main_risk: Translation choices themselves inject differences; use multiple independent translations per concept to bound translator variance.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Multilingual conditioning is assumed to route to a shared semantic space where language is incidental.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong English-dominant training may collapse other languages onto English visual priors, making distributions boringly identical rather than culturally distinct.
fastest_falsification_experiment: ~2k generations per language for ~20 concepts plus tests: under a day on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Spatial prepositions are executed by 2D canvas priors, not relational understanding: 'X above Y' succeeds only when the pair's canonical canvas arrangement agrees, and fails at predictable rates under counterfactual arrangements.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Spatial-relation prompts work impressively in demos and fail unpredictably in use; benchmarks report aggregate accuracy without separating relational competence from co-occurrence priors.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The model resolves spatial prepositions by sampling the most frequent canvas arrangement of the object pair from training statistics; genuine relational control exists only weakly, so accuracy collapses when the requested relation contradicts the canonical arrangement.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Accuracy on canonical-relation prompts (bird above fence) will exceed counter-canonical prompts (fence above bird) by at least 30 points across a balanced benchmark; kill if the canonicality gap is under 10 points (real relational control).
why_important: It separates 'knows the relation' from 'knows the world's typical layouts', the distinction that matters for any application needing controllable composition.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Spatial benchmarks exist; a canonicality-controlled counterfactual design isolating priors from relations appears rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build object pairs with strong canonical arrangements (from detection-corpus statistics), prompt both directions, score with detectors, and compare canonical versus counter-canonical accuracy.
main_risk: Counter-canonical scenes are also harder to render plausibly, so a rendering-difficulty control (e.g., synthetic-composite feasibility check) is needed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported spatial-relation accuracy is read as (imperfect but real) relational understanding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Newer models with layout-aware training may pass counter-canonical tests, making this a model-generation-specific result.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Balanced benchmark of ~1k prompt pairs with automated scoring: a few hours on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Conditioning modalities have a stable dominance hierarchy with measurable exchange rates: when text and structural conditions (edges, pose, depth) conflict, the resolution follows a lawful ordering that predicts multi-condition behavior before running it.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multi-condition generation (text plus structural control) is deployed everywhere, but what happens under condition conflict is undocumented beyond anecdote.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Each conditioning channel exerts influence proportional to its information rate about pixels and its injection depth; conflicts resolve by a consistent dominance ordering (dense structural > sparse structural > text) with quantifiable exchange rates that are stable across content.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In controlled conflict batteries (text says left, pose says right), structural conditions will win at least 75% of conflicts against text at default strengths, and fitted exchange rates (strength units of one condition per unit of another) will predict held-out conflict outcomes within 15%; kill if dominance is content-dependent and unstable (prediction error over 35%).
why_important: A conflict-resolution law makes multi-condition systems designable rather than trial-and-error, and reveals how the denoiser arbitrates information sources.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Condition-strength knobs exist per method; a cross-channel dominance calibration with predictive exchange rates appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build conflict batteries across condition pairs at varied strengths, score outcomes with detectors, fit a dominance/exchange model, and validate on held-out conflicts.
main_risk: Different control implementations (adapter architectures) may carry idiosyncratic strengths, requiring per-implementation calibration.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Condition interactions are assumed method-specific and not lawful across content and channels.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Arbitration may happen at semantic rather than channel level, with the winner varying by what is being contested.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Conflict batteries of ~3k generations: under a day on one GPU with public control adapters.

one_line_idea: Negation blindness lives in the text encoder, not the denoiser: negated prompts embed nearly identically to their affirmative forms, and embedding-level surgery fixes more negation failures than any sampling-time intervention.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Prompts like 'a street with no cars' notoriously produce cars, and fixes are attempted at sampling time (negative prompts, guidance tricks) with mixed results.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Contrastively trained text encoders map negated phrases close to affirmative ones (negation words carry little visual-embedding weight), so the denoiser never receives the negation; interventions that re-inject negation at the embedding level will dominate sampling-time fixes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Embedding similarity between negated and affirmative prompt pairs will exceed 0.9 (matched-scale baseline pairs at ~0.7), and embedding-space negation surgery will fix at least 2x more negation failures than tuned negative prompting at matched off-target change; kill if negated pairs are well separated (under 0.8) or embedding surgery underperforms sampling fixes.
why_important: Correct bottleneck localization redirects effort: if the encoder erases negation, all sampling-time work is patching downstream of an information loss.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Negation weakness of contrastive text encoders is discussed in VLM contexts; the causal chain into generation with an embedding-surgery comparison appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure negated/affirmative embedding geometry for a prompt battery, then compare negation-success rates for embedding-level interventions versus sampling-time fixes under matched image-change budgets.
main_risk: Embedding surgery may break other prompt content (entanglement), demanding careful off-target accounting.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Negation failure is treated as a generation-control problem to be fixed with negative prompts and guidance tricks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The denoiser might ignore even well-separated negation embeddings because training images virtually never depict 'absence' as a labeled property.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Embedding analysis is minutes; intervention comparison over ~1k prompts is a few hours on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Prompt rewriting by users converges on a folk grammar that works for lawful reasons: quantifying which rewrite operations (reordering, splitting, weighting) causally change generation shows most folk tricks are placebo while a small set has large, consistent effects.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Prompt-engineering folklore (word order tricks, emphasis syntax, quality tags) spreads through user communities with no causal evaluation, and model developers neither confirm nor refute it.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Only rewrite operations that change the embedding geometry meaningfully (content-word placement, splitting compound clauses) causally affect outputs, while popular decorations (quality tags, emphasis punctuation) have effects indistinguishable from resampling noise on modern models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In seed-controlled paired tests, at least half of the ten most popular folk tricks will show effect sizes below resampling noise (paired distribution shift indistinguishable at n=500), while content-reordering operations show significant effects in 80%+ of prompt families; kill if most folk tricks show robust significant effects (folk wisdom vindicated).
why_important: Prompt folklore consumes enormous user effort and contaminates model comparisons (different communities use different incantations); a causal audit cleans both.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt-engineering guides abound; seed-controlled causal effect-size measurement of folk operations appears rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Codify popular rewrite operations, apply them to a stratified prompt corpus with fixed seeds, and measure paired output changes against a resampling-noise baseline with automated and human metrics.
main_risk: Effects may be model-version-specific, requiring the audit to run on at least two model generations to say anything durable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Users believe the folk grammar reflects real model mechanics; developers privately assume most of it is superstition; neither side has measured it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Older models may genuinely respond to quality tags via training-data correlations, making 'placebo' a claim only about newer models.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Paired generation battery of ~10k images: about a day on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Distillation eats the tails first: few-step students lose rare modes (uncommon classes, unusual compositions) long before average-quality metrics degrade, following a lawful tail-truncation order predictable from teacher mode mass.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Few-step distilled models are validated on aggregate quality and preference scores, which are dominated by typical content and structurally blind to rare-mode loss.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Distillation objectives weight learning by probability mass, so student coverage shrinks from the tails inward: mode-level recall falls in inverse order of teacher mode mass, with a measurable truncation frontier that advances as steps decrease.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In class-conditional settings, rare-class generation recall will drop by 30%+ relative at 4 steps while common-class recall stays within 5%, and the recall-versus-mass curve will shift monotonically with step count; kill if losses are mass-uniform (rare and common classes degrade within 10% of each other).
why_important: Deployments switching to distilled models inherit an invisible diversity tax; a truncation law makes the tax measurable and negotiable (which tails to protect).
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Distillation papers report aggregate metrics; a mass-stratified mode-recall law appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Distill class-conditional models at several step budgets, measure per-class generation recall with a trained classifier, stratify by class frequency, and fit the truncation frontier.
main_risk: Classifier-based recall measurement has its own rare-class weakness; validate the measurement on held-out real images first.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Distillation is presented as a near-lossless speed trade at moderate step counts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some distillation families (distribution-matching objectives) may preserve tails better, making the law recipe-specific.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Small class-conditional distillation grid: roughly 3-5 GPU-days on one GPU with public data and models.

one_line_idea: Few-step students lose input sensitivity, not just diversity: the Jacobian of output with respect to conditioning collapses under distillation, predicting that distilled models are disproportionately worse for editing and control than for prompted generation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Distilled models are marketed as drop-in fast replacements, and controllability degradation is reported anecdotally without a mechanism or a measurement standard.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Compressing an iterative refinement into few steps forces the student toward locally flat input-output maps (small condition-Jacobian), so fine-grained condition changes (prompt tweaks, control-signal deltas) produce weaker, coarser output changes than the teacher's.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Condition-perturbation response (output change per unit prompt-embedding change) will be at least 40% lower in 1-4 step students than teachers, and the response deficit will predict editing-benchmark degradation across models at rank correlation 0.5+; kill if response magnitudes are within 15% of teachers.
why_important: It gives a mechanism and a cheap proxy for 'distilled models edit badly', informing which applications can and cannot adopt fast models.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Speed-quality tradeoffs are quantified; a sensitivity-collapse account with predictive validation appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure output responses to controlled condition perturbations for teacher-student pairs, then correlate response statistics with performance on standard editing/control tasks.
main_risk: Response magnitude is not automatically the right functional measure; complement with direction-alignment metrics between teacher and student responses.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Distillation is assumed to preserve the conditional map, merely accelerating its evaluation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some students may preserve sensitivity in semantic directions while collapsing only nuisance directions, which would be a positive finding against the hypothesis.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Perturbation-response measurement on public teacher-student pairs: a few hours on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Distillation concentrates memorization: few-step students reproduce the teacher's memorized items at equal or higher rates while losing non-memorized diversity, so the privacy-risk fraction of outputs increases through the very process meant to cheapen deployment.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Privacy audits target base models; distilled variants ship widely under the assumption that they inherit at most the teacher's leakage.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Memorized items are sharp high-mass attractors that distillation objectives preserve preferentially, while diffuse novel modes are pruned; the student's output distribution therefore over-represents memorized content relative to the teacher.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For known-memorized prompts, student near-copy rates will match or exceed teacher rates (ratio 1.0+), while student output diversity on neutral prompts drops 20%+, raising the memorized fraction of output mass by at least 1.5x; kill if student extraction rates fall by 30%+ alongside diversity (uniform compression).
why_important: If distillation amplifies the memorized fraction, every privacy audit done on teachers understates shipped-model risk, an actionable and testable compliance gap.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Memorization studies and distillation studies exist separately; their interaction appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare near-copy rates on known-memorized prompts and diversity on neutral prompts between public teacher-student pairs, and replicate with a controlled small-scale distillation of a model with planted duplicates.
main_risk: Public students differ from teachers in data and tricks beyond distillation; the controlled replicate carries the attribution weight.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Students are assumed to be lossy compressions whose losses apply to memorized and novel content alike.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Few-step dynamics may fail to reach sharp attractors (needing many steps to descend into them), actually reducing extraction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Teacher-student extraction comparison on known items: a few hours on one GPU; the planted replicate adds ~2 GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Guidance baked into distilled weights freezes the alignment-diversity operating point: no inference-time knob recovers the diversity a guidance-distilled student gave up, proving the tradeoff became structural rather than parametric.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Guidance distillation folds classifier-free guidance into student weights for speed, fixing the effective guidance scale at training time; whether the lost flexibility is recoverable is unknown.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Post-distillation, the diversity-alignment tradeoff is embedded in the learned map itself: sampling-time interventions (temperature-like noise scaling, early stopping, seed dithering) will fail to recover more than a small fraction of the teacher's accessible diversity range at matched alignment.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The area of the alignment-diversity region reachable by knob sweeps on a guidance-distilled student will be under 30% of the teacher's reachable region; kill if any knob combination recovers 60%+ of the teacher's operating range.
why_important: Deployments need to know whether choosing a distilled model is choosing a single operating point forever; it also clarifies what kind of object a guidance-distilled model is (a conditional distribution, not a family).
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Guidance distillation is established by recall; the reachable-region analysis of post-hoc flexibility appears new.

main_risk: Region area depends on metric choices for alignment and diversity; report under two independent metric pairs.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Recent students trained across guidance scales (scale-conditioned) may retain the full family, restricting the claim to scale-fixed distillates.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Knob sweeps of ~20k generations across configurations: about a day on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Distillation error concentrates in a measurable SNR band, so hybrid schedules that spend the few available steps non-uniformly (dense where teacher curvature is high) beat uniform few-step schedules at matched compute.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Few-step students conventionally place their steps uniformly or by inherited heuristics, and distillation losses are reported as global numbers without localization along the trajectory.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The student's disagreement with its teacher is not uniform over noise levels but peaks where the teacher's trajectory curvature is high; allocating student steps by measured disagreement mass recovers a meaningful fraction of the distillation loss for free.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Teacher-student disagreement profiles will show 50%+ of total disagreement mass concentrated in under 25% of the SNR range, and disagreement-weighted step placement will improve student quality by 10%+ relative at matched step count; kill if disagreement is flat (no band holds more than 35% of mass) or reallocation gains are under 3%.
why_important: A free quality recovery for every few-step deployment, plus a diagnostic (disagreement profile) that turns distillation debugging from guesswork into measurement.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Trajectory-localized distillation-error analysis with schedule reallocation appears unexplored; existing work tunes objectives, not step placement, by such profiles.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure per-SNR teacher-student output disagreement on a probe set, construct disagreement-weighted step schedules, and benchmark against uniform schedules at 2-8 steps.
main_risk: Student architectures trained for specific step placements may need light re-tuning for new schedules, complicating the matched-compute comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Step placement for few-step models is treated as a solved detail inherited from samplers, not a distillation-specific optimization surface.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Consistency-trained students may equalize error over noise levels by construction, flattening the profile the method needs.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Disagreement profiling plus schedule benchmark on public teacher-student pairs: about a day on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Violation of the semigroup property (two 1-step jumps disagreeing with one 2-step jump) is an intrinsic inconsistency measure for few-step models that tracks their distillation quality without any reference images or teacher access.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Evaluating distilled models requires reference sets, teacher access, or preference studies; there is no intrinsic self-consistency diagnostic computable from the student alone.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] An ideal few-step model's jumps compose consistently (the flow-map semigroup property); real students violate it in proportion to how badly distillation compressed the trajectory, so composition error is a reference-free proxy of distillation loss.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across students of varying known quality (different recipes/budgets from the same teacher), mean composition error will rank-correlate with reference-based quality gaps at 0.6+; kill if correlation is under 0.3 (composition error measures something orthogonal to quality).
why_important: A teacher-free, data-free diagnostic would let practitioners monitor distillation during training and compare shipped students without expensive evaluation harnesses. This measures the model's internal consistency as a scientific property, not as a content detector.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Consistency losses are used in training; composition error as a post-hoc quality instrument with validated correlation appears unformalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Produce a ladder of students at varying distillation budgets, compute composition-error statistics on random inputs for each, and correlate with reference-based quality measurements.
main_risk: Students trained with explicit consistency objectives may minimize exactly this quantity without fixing quality, decoupling the proxy for that recipe family.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Model quality is assumed to require external references; internal consistency is treated as a training trick, not a measurement.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Composition error may saturate quickly with quality, discriminating bad students from terrible ones but not good from great.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Composition-error computation is minutes per student; the student ladder is the cost, roughly 3-4 GPU-days at small scale.

one_line_idea: Teacher-student representational alignment early in distillation predicts final student quality: CKA at matched noise levels after a small fraction of training forecasts the outcome, enabling early stopping of doomed distillation runs.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Distillation runs are expensive and their final quality varies with recipe and hyperparameters in ways discovered only at the end.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Successful distillation proceeds by first aligning internal representations and then refining outputs; early representational alignment (CKA between teacher and student features at matched SNR) is therefore a leading indicator of final output quality.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] CKA measured at 10% of training will predict final quality across a grid of recipes with rank correlation 0.6+, beating early output-loss values as a predictor by a significant margin; kill if early CKA predicts no better than early loss (correlation advantage under 0.1).
why_important: A validated early-stopping signal would save large fractions of distillation compute across the industry and support the representational-first theory of how distillation works.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] CKA is standard for representation comparison; its use as an early predictive signal for distillation outcomes appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a grid of small-scale distillations with varied recipes, log CKA and loss trajectories, and evaluate early-signal predictiveness of final quality.
main_risk: Prediction may hold within a recipe family but fail across families, limiting the tool to hyperparameter search rather than recipe selection.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Early training signals are assumed uninformative for final generative quality; practitioners run to completion.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Output quality may hinge on late-phase phenomena (e.g., mode consolidation) invisible to early representational similarity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: A grid of ~10 small distillations with periodic CKA logging: roughly 5 GPU-days on one GPU.

one_line_idea: One-step generators are qualitatively different objects from few-step ones: the 1-to-2 step transition shows a discontinuous jump in output-map smoothness and failure structure, while 2-to-8 steps vary smoothly, locating the real boundary of 'diffusion-like' behavior.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Step-count comparisons treat 1, 2, 4, 8 steps as points on one quality curve, implicitly assuming the underlying computation degrades smoothly toward fewer steps.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] With two or more steps the model retains an intermediate-correction mechanism (see noise, adjust) that a single-step map structurally lacks; measurable properties (input-Jacobian spectra, artifact taxonomy, OOD-prompt behavior) will show a discontinuity between 1 and 2 steps and smooth variation beyond.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across matched students, the 1-to-2 step gap in Jacobian-spectrum statistics and artifact-class distributions will exceed the 2-to-4 and 4-to-8 gaps by at least 2x; kill if all successive gaps are within 30% of each other (smooth family).
why_important: If one-step models are categorically different, research on 'few-step' methods should split into two problems with different theory and different failure modes, and deployment risk assessments should not interpolate across the boundary.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Step-quality curves are ubiquitous; a structural-discontinuity analysis of the 1-to-2 transition appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or obtain students at 1, 2, 4, 8 steps from one teacher, measure Jacobian statistics, artifact taxonomies (via automated artifact classifiers plus human audit), and OOD-prompt degradation, comparing successive-step gaps.
main_risk: Artifact taxonomy construction is subjective; anchor it with automated classifiers trained on synthetic artifact injections.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Step count is treated as a continuous quality dial with 1 step as merely its cheapest setting.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern one-step distillates with strong regularization may already close the structural gap, making the discontinuity historical.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Using public multi-step student releases where available, the measurement suite is about a day on one GPU; training a controlled ladder adds ~4 GPU-days at small scale.

one_line_idea: Latent compression sets a hard fidelity floor for small structures: objects below a critical pixel size cannot be faithfully generated by 8x-downsampling latent models regardless of denoiser scale, and the decode(encode(x)) roundtrip bound cleanly attributes such failures to the VAE, not the denoiser.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Latent diffusion systems fail on small text, faces in crowds, and thin structures, and these failures are routinely blamed on the denoiser or prompt without separating the autoencoder's contribution.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The VAE roundtrip decode(encode(x)) is an upper bound on achievable fidelity per structure size; measured roundtrip fidelity will show a critical size below which information is destroyed, and generation failures on small structures will track this bound rather than denoiser capacity.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Roundtrip legibility/identity of structures below the critical size (estimated around 8-16 pixels for common 8x VAEs) will fall under 50% while generation failures on matched structures occur at rates within 15 points of the roundtrip bound across two denoiser scales; kill if bigger denoisers beat the roundtrip bound (impossible under the hypothesis) or failures are uncorrelated with roundtrip fidelity.
why_important: A clean VAE-versus-denoiser attribution protocol redirects engineering investment (retrain the autoencoder versus scale the denoiser) and quantifies a structural ceiling every latent generator shares.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] VAE lossiness is known qualitatively; a size-resolved roundtrip bound used as an attribution instrument for generation failures appears unformalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure structure-size-resolved roundtrip fidelity (rendered text, faces, gratings at controlled sizes) for public VAEs, then measure generation fidelity on prompts requiring those structures across denoiser scales, and compare against the bound.
main_risk: Generation can sidestep the bound by making structures larger than requested, so size compliance must be measured and controlled.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Small-structure failures are treated as denoiser or data limitations that model scaling will fix.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Denoisers might exploit latent-space redundancy to encode sub-latent detail in distributed form, beating naive roundtrip expectations.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Roundtrip battery plus generation battery: a few hours on one GPU with public checkpoints.

one_line_idea: Latent space is perceptually non-uniform: equal latent distances correspond to wildly different perceptual changes across image regions and content types, distorting every latent-space loss, edit magnitude, and interpolation built on it.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Methods routinely treat latent L2 distances as meaningful (losses, edit strengths, interpolation paths), assuming the VAE latent is a perceptually calibrated space.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The VAE's compression objective allocates latent resolution by reconstruction difficulty, not perceptual salience, so the local latent-to-perceptual metric ratio varies by an order of magnitude across content (faces versus sky), making latent distances systematically misleading.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The measured local metric ratio (perceptual change per unit latent change) will vary by at least 5x between high-salience and low-salience content regions, and latent-distance-based edit strength will misestimate perceptual edit magnitude by 2x+ for at least 30% of images; kill if metric ratios vary under 2x (space approximately uniform).
why_important: Quantifying the distortion would explain systematic edit-strength inconsistencies across content and enable a corrected (perceptually reweighted) latent metric usable by all latent-space methods.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Perceptual non-uniformity is established for pixel and GAN latent spaces; a measured metric-tensor census for diffusion VAEs with downstream correction appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate local metric ratios via controlled latent perturbations decoded and scored perceptually across a stratified image set, map ratio statistics by content type, and test a reweighted metric on edit-strength calibration.
main_risk: Perceptual metrics themselves are imperfect; use two independent perceptual measures plus a small human check.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Latent distances are treated as a serviceable proxy for perceptual distances because the VAE was trained with perceptual losses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Perceptual-loss training may have flattened the metric more than hypothesized, making latent L2 roughly honest after all.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Perturbation-decode battery over ~2k images: a few hours on one GPU.

one_line_idea: VAE decoders hallucinate texture deterministically: the fake high-frequency detail added during decoding is a repeatable function of latent content (not random), meaning latent generators systematically sign their outputs with decoder-specific texture and cannot represent certain true textures at all.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] VAE decoders synthesize high-frequency detail the latent cannot carry, and this hallucinated texture is treated as harmless stochastic garnish.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Decoder texture synthesis is deterministic given the latent: repeated decodes and near-duplicate latents produce near-identical fake texture, implying a fixed texture vocabulary that (a) fingerprints the decoder and (b) excludes textures outside its vocabulary from ever being generated faithfully.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Texture patches from decodes of perturbed latents will show self-similarity far above real-texture baselines (feature-space similarity 2x+ the natural-variation baseline), and a held-out texture-classification probe will identify the decoder from output patches at 80%+ accuracy across 4 public VAEs; kill if decoder identification is near chance or texture varies like natural texture.
why_important: Deterministic hallucination defines what latent generators can never faithfully produce (a capability boundary) and explains texture monotony complaints; the decoder-vocabulary concept gives autoencoder training a measurable target.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Decoder artifacts are discussed informally; determinism, vocabulary structure, and cross-decoder fingerprinting as a capability boundary appear unstudied. This characterizes generator limitations, not a content-detection scheme.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Decode perturbed-latent ensembles, quantify texture self-similarity versus natural baselines, train decoder-identification probes across public VAEs, and catalog texture families each decoder can and cannot reproduce from matched real patches.
main_risk: Distinguishing 'decoder vocabulary' from faithful reconstruction requires ground-truth textures the latent provably cannot carry; construct these with sub-latent-resolution synthetic textures.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Decoder detail synthesis is assumed benignly stochastic and content-appropriate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adversarially trained decoders may synthesize genuinely diverse texture conditioned on subtle latent cues, dissolving the fixed-vocabulary picture.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Perturb-decode ensembles plus probes across public VAEs: under a day on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Latent channels carry stable global roles (luma-like, chroma-like, detail-like) consistent across images, so channel-targeted interventions provide training-free global controls (exposure, palette, detail level) with predictable effects.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The latent channels of common VAEs are treated as an uninterpretable code; all control is exercised through prompts, conditioning adapters, or fine-tuning.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Compression pressure plus image statistics push VAEs toward a decorrelated color-like basis: individual channels (or fixed linear combinations) will have consistent global functions across content, making channel arithmetic a reliable control surface.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Fixed channel-space directions will produce the same nameable global effect (e.g., brightness, warmth) on 80%+ of diverse images with off-target structural change below a perceptual threshold, and these directions will transfer across images without per-image search; kill if effects are content-dependent (consistent on under 40%) or structurally destructive.
why_important: A free, universal, interpretable control surface for every latent-diffusion deployment, plus evidence about what structure VAE compression discovers.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Channel-meaning folklore circulates in practitioner communities; a systematic census with consistency statistics and transfer tests appears unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply fixed channel-direction offsets across a stratified image set, score effect consistency with automated attribute measures, and test transfer of discovered directions to held-out images and a second VAE.
main_risk: Roles may hold for global statistics but interact with the denoiser during generation (versus post-hoc editing), requiring both settings to be tested separately.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Latent channels are assumed entangled and uninterpretable, with control requiring learned adapters.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Higher-channel-count VAEs may distribute roles redundantly, giving no single-direction handles.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Channel-offset battery over ~1k images and two VAEs: a few hours on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Sampled latents sometimes leave the decoder-valid region, producing a distinct artifact family; a cheap latent-typicality projection at the final step removes these artifacts without retraining anything.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Latent generators occasionally emit characteristic artifacts (blocky corruption, color explosions) whose cause is debated and whose fixes are ad hoc (reroll the seed).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The denoiser can terminate at latents outside the encoder's output distribution (where the decoder was never trained); artifact occurrences will coincide with measurable latent atypicality, and projecting final latents toward the encoder-output manifold will remove the artifact family with minimal content change.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Artifact-flagged generations will show latent-typicality scores in the extreme tail (bottom decile) at 3x+ the base rate, and typicality projection will fix 60%+ of flagged cases with content change below an edit-magnitude threshold; kill if artifacts are uncorrelated with typicality (under 1.3x enrichment).
why_important: It attributes a whole artifact family to a specific mechanism (latent-manifold escape) and ships a train-free fix applicable to every latent generator.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Latent-space out-of-distribution effects on decoders are plausible folklore; the enrichment measurement plus projection fix appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit a typicality model on encoder outputs over a public image corpus, score generated latents, correlate artifact flags (automated plus human audit) with typicality, and evaluate the projection fix on flagged cases.
main_risk: Artifact flagging is the weakest link; combine an automated detector with a human-audited subsample to calibrate flag quality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Such artifacts are blamed on the denoiser having 'bad seeds' rather than on a decoder-domain mismatch.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Artifacts may originate mid-trajectory in the denoiser itself, with final-latent atypicality a symptom that projection cannot fix.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Typicality scoring plus projection over ~20k generations: under a day on one GPU.

one_line_idea: The shared-VAE ecosystem correlates errors across 'independent' models: generators built on the same public autoencoder share failure modes and texture signatures, so ensembling them recovers far less than ensemble theory predicts.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many public generators reuse a small number of pretrained VAEs, and users ensemble or cross-check such models assuming their errors are independent.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The shared decoder imposes shared blind spots (texture vocabulary, small-structure floor, color quirks); error correlation between same-VAE model pairs will substantially exceed correlation between different-VAE pairs, and same-VAE ensembles will underperform predicted ensemble gains.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On structure-fidelity and texture tasks, same-VAE model pairs will show error correlations at least 0.2 higher than different-VAE pairs, and same-VAE ensembling will realize under half the error-reduction predicted by independence; kill if correlation differences are under 0.05.
why_important: Ecosystem-level dependence breaks the independence assumptions behind ensembling, model cross-validation, and 'multiple models agree' arguments throughout generative-model practice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Component sharing is public knowledge; its quantitative consequence for error correlation and ensemble value appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select model pairs stratified by VAE sharing, measure per-item errors on structure/texture batteries, compute correlation matrices, and compare ensemble gains against independence predictions.
main_risk: Same-VAE models also often share training data and architectures; a data-controlled subset or decoder-swap experiment is needed to isolate the VAE's share.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Differently branded models are assumed to be effectively independent draws for the purpose of ensembling and agreement checks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The denoiser and data may dominate error structure so completely that the decoder's shared contribution is negligible.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Error batteries across ~6 public models: about a day on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Decoder swapping is a causal attribution instrument: decoding one model's latents with another compatible decoder cleanly splits every output property (artifact, texture, color bias) into denoiser-caused versus decoder-caused, with percentage attributions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] When a latent generator misbehaves, teams cannot tell whether to retrain the denoiser or the autoencoder, because outputs entangle both components.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For VAEs trained on similar data with compatible latent conventions, cross-decoding is faithful enough that property changes under decoder swap measure the decoder's causal share of each output property, yielding a reusable attribution protocol.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Decoder swaps will attribute at least 70% of texture-family signatures to the decoder and at least 70% of layout/content properties to the denoiser (double dissociation), with attribution stable (within 10 points) across image sets; kill if cross-decoding is too lossy to preserve content (making attribution meaningless) or attributions are unstable.
why_important: A validated component-attribution instrument converts 'the model is weird' bug reports into targeted engineering, and maps which output properties live where in the latent-generation stack.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Decoder swaps are occasionally done ad hoc for compatibility; formalizing swap-based causal attribution with stability criteria appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify decoder pairs with compatible latent spaces (or fit light latent adapters), generate matched sets, decode under both decoders, and measure per-property deltas with stability checks across content strata.
main_risk: Latent-convention incompatibility may require adapters whose own effects contaminate attribution; adapter-free same-family pairs are the clean starting point.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Output properties are treated as belonging to 'the model' as a monolith, with attribution considered impractical.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Denoisers may adapt during training to their specific decoder's quirks, entangling the components beyond what swaps can separate.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Swap battery over ~5k generations and 2-3 decoder pairs: a few hours on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Coarse-to-fine generation is an artifact of Gaussian noise schedules, not an intrinsic property of diffusion: alternative corruption operators reorder which image structure is decided when, causing predictable trades between layout errors and texture errors.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Diffusion models are described as intrinsically coarse-to-fine generators, and this narrative shapes architecture and schedule design, yet the property is only ever demonstrated under Gaussian corruption.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The generation order of spatial frequencies is fully determined by the corruption operator's frequency-versus-time SNR profile; corruptions that destroy low frequencies first will produce fine-to-coarse generation and correspondingly shifted error profiles (more layout errors, fewer texture errors).
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Models trained with low-frequency-first corruption will decide texture before layout in trajectory-swap probes (reversal of the standard commitment order in 70%+ of cases) and will show at least 20% relative more layout-inconsistency errors with correspondingly fewer texture errors; kill if generation order stays coarse-to-fine regardless of corruption.
why_important: If the celebrated coarse-to-fine story is schedule-induced, corruption design becomes a task-alignment tool (choose the ordering your task needs) rather than a fixed doctrine.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Alternative corruptions have been explored for quality by recall; the decision-order and error-profile consequences appear unmapped.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train small models under Gaussian, blur-first, and band-reversed corruptions on public data, run commitment-order probes and error-taxonomy scoring on generations from each.
main_risk: Alternative corruptions may simply train worse, confounding order effects with quality collapse; match models at equal sample quality where possible.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Coarse-to-fine is treated as an inherent virtue of diffusion explaining its structural coherence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Network inductive biases (convolution, attention locality) may impose coarse-to-fine ordering independently of the corruption profile.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three small trainings plus probes at CIFAR scale: about 3-4 GPU-days on one GPU with public data.

one_line_idea: Diffusion models under-generate high-frequency power with a lawful spectral deficit: the gap between generated and real power spectra has a stable shape per model family, predicting which fine-structure content will systematically look 'smoothed'.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Generated images often look subtly smooth or plasticky, an observation discussed via anecdote and single-metric comparisons rather than a quantitative spectral law.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Training dynamics and finite sampling systematically under-fit the highest frequency octaves; the relative spectral deficit curve (generated over real power versus frequency) is stable across content categories within a model and shifts predictably with sampling steps and model scale.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The spectral deficit curve will be reproducible across disjoint content categories within a model (curve correlation 0.8+), with top-octave deficits of 10%+ that shrink monotonically with sampling steps; kill if deficits are content-idiosyncratic (correlation under 0.4) or absent at convergence.
why_important: A stable deficit law identifies which applications (fine textures, distant detail) inherit systematic bias from generated imagery and provides a spectral target for training and sampling fixes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Spectral discrepancies of GANs were studied; a schedule/steps-resolved deficit law for modern diffusion systems appears incompletely characterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute radially averaged spectra for large generated and real sets matched by content category, fit deficit curves per category, model, and step count, and test curve stability.
main_risk: Real-data spectra vary with camera pipelines; matching content and processing between real and generated sets is essential.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Smoothness is attributed vaguely to 'model limitations' without a reproducible quantitative structure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Latent-space models may show decoder-dominated spectra (from the texture vocabulary) rather than a clean denoiser-driven deficit, complicating the law.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Spectral analysis over ~50k generated plus matched real images: a few hours on one GPU.

one_line_idea: Terminal-SNR mismatch produces a quantifiable brightness/mean-shift artifact: the residual signal at the schedule's terminal step leaks into every generation as a predictable global bias, computable in closed form from the schedule and verifiable across public models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Schedules that do not reach zero SNR at the terminal step train the model on a mismatch (the 'noise' still contains signal), and zero-terminal-SNR fixes exist, but the artifact's quantitative structure across the model zoo is undocumented.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The terminal residual acts as a fixed prior injected into all generations; its magnitude and direction (mean brightness, low-frequency bias) are computable from the schedule's terminal statistics and will predict measured generation biases model by model.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Predicted mean-shift magnitudes from terminal-SNR values will match measured generation mean biases across 5+ public models with rank correlation 0.7+, and zero-terminal-SNR models will show biases below half the nonzero-terminal group's median; kill if predicted and measured biases are uncorrelated (under 0.3).
why_important: It converts a known training mismatch into a predictive quantitative account, letting practitioners diagnose schedule-induced bias from config files without running experiments.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The zero-terminal-SNR issue is published by recall; the cross-model predictive-bias law appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract schedule parameters from public model configs, compute predicted terminal-residual biases, generate large unconditional/neutral-prompt sets per model, and compare measured global statistics against predictions.
main_risk: Post-hoc fixes (rescaling tricks in pipelines) may mask the raw effect; test with pipeline corrections disabled where possible.
